tool.name: Google Analytics
tool.tagline: Measure how people find and use your website with Google Analytics 4
tool.description: Google Analytics 4 (GA4) is Google's free web and app analytics product. A small tag on your site sends events to a property, and GA4 turns them into reports about traffic sources, engagement, conversions and revenue, plus the Explore workspace for ad-hoc analysis. Learning it well means knowing the event data model, instrumenting a site correctly, and reading and building the right reports and explorations.

concepts.name: What Google Analytics 4 is
concepts.summary: GA4 is Google's event-based analytics product that replaced Universal Analytics in 2023.
concepts.why: Knowing what GA4 measures and how it differs from the old product tells you what its numbers mean.
concepts.body:
**Google Analytics 4** (GA4) is the current version of Google Analytics. You add a small JavaScript tag to your website (or the Firebase SDK to an app), the tag sends **events** to Google, and GA4 turns those events into reports about who visits, where they came from, what they did and whether they converted.

It replaced **Universal Analytics** (UA). UA stopped processing data on 1 July 2023 and its historical data was deleted in 2024, so anything you read about "goals", "bounce rate as a top metric" or "hit types" describes the old product. The differences matter:

- UA stored pageviews, events and transactions as different hit types. GA4 stores *everything* as an event with parameters: a page view is just the `page_view` event.
- UA was session-centric; GA4 is user- and event-centric, and can tie web and app data together in one property.
- GA4 reports come in two families: curated **standard reports** and the free-form **Explore** workspace for ad-hoc analysis.
- GA4 uses machine-learned modelling (for consented-but-missing data and predictive metrics) rather than only raw counts.

GA4 is free for most sites; a paid tier, **Analytics 360**, raises limits (sampling thresholds, retention, export volume). Everything in this course applies to the free tier unless noted.

People use GA4 to answer questions like: which campaigns bring buyers, which landing pages lose people, where users drop out of a signup flow, and how many of last month's new users came back.
takeaways: GA4 is event-based: every interaction, including a page view, is an event
Universal Analytics is dead since July 2023; its vocabulary (goals, hit types) does not apply
Two ways to look at data: standard reports and Explore

quiz.q: How does GA4 record a page view?
options: As a page_view event with parameters
As a special pageview hit type
Only in Realtime, not in reports
quiz.explain: GA4 has one data type, the event; a page view is the page_view event with parameters like page_location.

concepts.name: Accounts, properties and data streams
concepts.summary: An account holds properties; a property holds data streams; a web stream gives you the G- measurement ID.
concepts.why: You cannot install or administer GA4 without knowing which of the three layers a setting lives on.
concepts.body:
GA4 has a three-level hierarchy.

- An **account** is the top-level container, usually one per company. It owns billing-style settings such as data-sharing options and account-level user access.
- A **property** is where data lives and reports are built. One property normally equals one business or product, and it can combine a website and its mobile apps. Time zone, currency, data retention, key events, audiences and custom definitions are all property settings.
- A **data stream** is a source of events inside the property: a *web* stream for a site, an *iOS* or *Android* stream for an app. A web stream has a **measurement ID** that looks like `G-ABC123XYZ`; that is what the tag on your pages sends to.

A common mistake is creating one property per website section or per country when you want to compare them in one report. Use a single property and split with dimensions (hostname, page path, country) instead; you cannot report across properties without BigQuery or a 360 roll-up property.

The **Admin** section (gear icon, bottom left) is split into an Account column and a Property column. Under Property you will spend most of your time in *Data collection and modification* (data streams, data filters, retention, deletion requests), *Data display* (events, key events, audiences, custom definitions, channel groups, attribution, reporting identity, DebugView) and *Product links* (Google Ads, Search Console, BigQuery).

Each web stream also has **Configure tag settings**, where tag-level behaviour such as internal traffic rules, cross-domain lists and session timeout is defined.
takeaways: Account > property > data stream; the web stream's G- ID is what you install
One property per business, not per site section; split with dimensions
Admin is organised into Account and Property columns

quiz.q: Where is data retention configured?
quiz.explain: Retention, key events, audiences and custom definitions are all property-level settings.

quiz.q: What does a measurement ID like G-ABC123XYZ identify?
quiz.explain: Each web data stream has its own G- measurement ID; app streams use Firebase app IDs.

concepts.name: Events and parameters
concepts.summary: Every interaction is an event with a name and key-value parameters; GA4 has four kinds of events.
concepts.why: The event model is the foundation of every report, exploration and custom definition you will ever build.
concepts.body:
In GA4 an **event** is a named record of something happening: `page_view`, `scroll`, `purchase`, `sign_up`. Each event carries **parameters**, key-value pairs that describe it: `page_location`, `value`, `currency`, `method`. Some parameters are added automatically to every event (`page_title`, `language`, `screen_resolution`, `ga_session_id`); others you send yourself.

There are four categories of events:

- **Automatically collected**: sent by the tag with no configuration, e.g. `first_visit`, `session_start`, `user_engagement`.
- **Enhanced measurement**: optional browser interactions you toggle on in the web stream, e.g. `scroll`, `click` (outbound), `file_download`, `video_start`.
- **Recommended**: events Google names and documents, with expected parameters, such as `login`, `sign_up`, `purchase` and `generate_lead`. Using these names unlocks prebuilt reports and features.
- **Custom**: anything else you name yourself, like `newsletter_toggle`.

Limits to remember: event names are up to 40 characters, case-sensitive and should be snake_case; an event can carry up to 25 custom parameters; a parameter value is up to 100 characters. Exceeding limits silently drops the extra data.

A parameter only shows up in reports if GA4 knows about it: the standard parameters are built in, while your own parameters must be registered as **custom dimensions** or **custom metrics** (covered later). Raw parameters are always visible in DebugView and BigQuery, which is why those two are your debugging friends.

Event-level data is what explorations work with; standard reports aggregate it into pre-computed tables.
takeaways: Event = name + parameters; parameters describe the event
Automatic, enhanced measurement, recommended, custom: in that order of effort
Custom parameters need a custom dimension/metric to appear in reports

quiz.q: You send a custom parameter plan_type with your sign_up event. Where will you see it immediately?
options: In the Events report as a column
In DebugView and BigQuery, but not in standard reports until registered
Nowhere until you create an audience
quiz.explain: Unregistered parameters are collected but only surface in DebugView/BigQuery; a custom dimension makes them reportable.

quiz.q: Which event category requires no configuration at all?
quiz.explain: first_visit, session_start and user_engagement are sent by the tag with no settings.

concepts.name: Users, sessions and engagement
concepts.summary: How GA4 counts users and sessions, and what makes a session or user 'engaged'.
concepts.why: Engagement rate replaced bounce rate as the headline quality metric, and users in GA4 mean active users by default.
concepts.body:
A **user** in GA4 is identified by a pseudonymous ID stored in the `_ga` cookie (or by your own User-ID; see reporting identity). GA4 reports three user metrics: *Total users* (anyone who logged an event), *New users* (fired `first_visit`), and *Active users*, which is what the plain "Users" column in standard reports means. A user is **active** if they had an engaged session or their first visit in the period.

A **session** starts with the automatic `session_start` event and ends after 30 minutes of inactivity (adjustable between 5 minutes and 7 hours 55 minutes in the web stream's tag settings). Unlike Universal Analytics, a session does not restart at midnight or when a new campaign parameter appears, so GA4 usually shows fewer sessions than UA did for the same site. Every event carries `ga_session_id` so GA4 can group them.

A session is **engaged** when at least one of these is true:

- it lasted longer than 10 seconds (adjustable up to 60 seconds in tag settings),
- it had a key event,
- it had two or more page views or screen views.

**Engagement rate** = engaged sessions / sessions. **Bounce rate** still exists but is simply 1 minus engagement rate. *Average engagement time* comes from the `user_engagement` event, which the tag sends with the time the page was actually in the foreground, so it is more honest than UA's time on page.

*Views per session* and *Sessions per user* round out the basic set. Because engagement is measured client-side, a user who reads a page for 2 minutes and leaves counts as engaged, which UA would have called a bounce.
takeaways: "Users" in reports means active users, not total users
Sessions time out after 30 minutes of inactivity and do not split at midnight
Engaged session: >10 s, or a key event, or 2+ page views; engagement rate is the headline

quiz.q: A visitor reads one page for 45 seconds and leaves. In GA4 the session is...
options: A bounce, since only one page was viewed
Engaged, because it lasted more than 10 seconds
Engaged only if a key event fired
quiz.explain: Any session over 10 seconds counts as engaged regardless of page count.

concepts.name: Dimensions, metrics and scope
concepts.summary: Dimensions describe, metrics count, and each belongs to a user, session, event or item scope.
concepts.why: Mixing scopes is the single most common reason a GA4 table looks wrong or shows (not set).
concepts.body:
Every table in GA4 is built from **dimensions** (text attributes: country, page path, event name, session source) and **metrics** (numbers: users, sessions, event count, revenue). You pick dimensions to break the data down and metrics to measure it.

Each dimension and metric has a **scope**, meaning which object it describes:

- **User** scope: attributes of the person, e.g. *First user source*, *Age*, *Lifetime value*, user properties.
- **Session** scope: attributes of a visit, e.g. *Session source / medium*, *Session default channel group*, *Landing page*, metric *Sessions*.
- **Event** scope: attributes of a single event, e.g. *Event name*, *Page location*, *Link URL*, metric *Event count*; most custom dimensions live here.
- **Item** scope: attributes of a product in an ecommerce `items` array, e.g. *Item name*, *Item brand*, metric *Item revenue*.

Combining scopes is allowed but can be meaningless. Breaking *Sessions* down by *Event name* asks "how many sessions contained each event", which is fine; breaking *Event count* for `purchase` down by *Landing page* is also fine because the landing page is attached to the session the event belongs to. But a session-scoped dimension against a user-scoped metric, or an item-scoped dimension against an event-scoped metric, produces either `(not set)` or inflated numbers because the join is not one-to-one.

A practical rule: start from the metric you want, then only add dimensions at the same scope or a wider one (event inside session inside user). GA4's dimension picker in Explore marks incompatible combinations, and standard reports simply refuse to add them.

`(not set)` in a row usually means the dimension had no value for those events, not that data was lost.
takeaways: Dimensions describe, metrics count; both have a scope
Scopes: user, session, event, item
Add dimensions at the same or wider scope than your metric to avoid (not set)

quiz.q: Which pairing is most likely to produce a misleading table?
quiz.explain: Item-scoped dimensions only describe the products inside ecommerce events; pairing them with a session metric does not join cleanly.

concepts.name: Reporting identity
concepts.summary: How GA4 decides that two events belong to the same person: User-ID, device ID and modelling.
concepts.why: Changing the identity setting silently changes your user counts and can trigger data thresholding.
concepts.body:
GA4 can recognise a person in several ways, called **identity spaces**:

- **User-ID**: an ID you send (`user_id` in the config or event) when someone is logged in. It is the only space that joins the same person across browsers and devices.
- **Device ID**: the `_ga` cookie's client ID on the web, or the app-instance ID on mobile. The default when nothing else is available.
- **Modelled data**: when users decline cookies under consent mode, GA4 can model their behaviour from consented users.

Until February 2024 **Google signals** (data from signed-in Google users who allow ads personalisation) was also part of identity. It no longer is: Google signals is still used for demographics, interests and remarketing audiences, but it does not stitch users for reporting any more.

In Admin > Reporting identity you pick how these spaces are combined:

- **Blended**: User-ID, then device ID, then modelled data. Default.
- **Observed**: User-ID, then device ID. No modelling.
- **Device-based**: device ID only; ignores User-ID.

The choice affects reports only, not collection, so you can switch back and forth: nothing is lost. Why switch? Because any identity space that could reveal individuals makes GA4 apply **data thresholding** (hiding small rows). If you see the thresholding warning icon in a report and need the full rows, temporarily switch to Device-based.

User-ID must not be personally identifiable (no emails), must be the same string everywhere, and user counts fall when you add it because cross-device duplicates collapse. That drop is correct, not a bug.
takeaways: Identity spaces: User-ID, device ID, modelled; Google signals left identity in 2024
Blended / Observed / Device-based are report-time settings, reversible
Thresholding is tied to identity; Device-based avoids it

quiz.q: You switch Reporting identity from Blended to Device-based. What happens to already-collected data?
options: Nothing; only how reports join events changes
It is reprocessed and permanently deduplicated
Events without a User-ID are deleted
quiz.explain: Reporting identity is applied at query time, so switching is non-destructive.

quiz.q: Which identity space can join the same person on a phone and a laptop?
quiz.explain: Only an ID you set when the person logs in survives across devices.

concepts.name: Installing the tag with gtag.js
concepts.summary: Paste the Google tag snippet into <head> on every page, or load GA4 through Google Tag Manager.
concepts.why: No tag, no data: this is the first thing you do on any site, and it decides where every later change happens.
concepts.body:
The simplest install is the **Google tag** snippet, shown in Admin > Data streams > your web stream > *View tag instructions*. It loads `gtag.js` asynchronously and configures it with your measurement ID. Put it as high in `<head>` as possible on every page, including error pages, so page views and timing are consistent.

The snippet does three things: loads the library, defines `dataLayer` and the `gtag()` function, and calls `gtag('config', 'G-...')`, which fires the first `page_view` and sets the `_ga` cookie. Options go in the config object: `send_page_view: false` to control page views yourself, `user_id` to set a User-ID, `debug_mode: true` to see events in DebugView.

The alternative is **Google Tag Manager** (GTM). You place one GTM container snippet on the site and create a *Google tag* (GA4 configuration) and GA4 event tags inside GTM's web UI. GTM wins when marketing needs to add or change tags without code deploys, or you have many vendors; `gtag.js` wins for a small site or one that developers fully control. Do not run both for the same measurement ID or every page view is doubled.

Frameworks (Next.js, Nuxt, Gatsby) and CMSs (WordPress, Shopify, Wix) usually have a plugin or a *Site Kit*-style integration that injects the same snippet; what matters is that exactly one tag with your G- ID runs per page.

After installing, open Realtime or DebugView and load the page: you should see yourself within seconds. Full report data takes 24 to 48 hours to settle.
concepts.code: Welcome
takeaways: One Google tag snippet in <head> on every page, or one GTM container
gtag('config', ...) fires the first page_view and accepts options
Never run gtag.js and a GTM Google tag for the same ID together
pitfalls: Installing the snippet twice (theme + plugin) and doubling every page view.

quiz.q: Why is the Google tag placed in <head> rather than at the end of <body>?
options: So page_view fires early and consistently before the user leaves
It would not work in body
head is required by HTML for scripts
It makes the page load faster
quiz.explain: The script is async, so it does not block; loading it early captures short visits reliably.

concepts.name: Enhanced measurement
concepts.summary: Toggle automatic scroll, outbound click, site search, video, file download and form events in the web stream.
concepts.why: It gives you most of the interaction events a marketing site needs without writing any code.
concepts.body:
**Enhanced measurement** is a set of switches on the web data stream (Admin > Data streams > stream > Enhanced measurement). When on, the tag listens to the browser and sends events for you:

- **Page views** (`page_view`), including an option to fire on browser history changes for single-page apps.
- **Scrolls** (`scroll`): fired once per page when the user reaches 90% depth. There is no 25/50/75 option; use GTM or custom code for that.
- **Outbound clicks** (`click` with `link_url`, `outbound: true`): links to a different domain. Domains in your cross-domain list are not outbound.
- **Site search** (`view_search_results` with `search_term`): triggered by a query parameter such as `q`, `s`, `search`, `query` or `keyword`; you can add your own.
- **Form interactions** (`form_start`, `form_submit`), with `form_id`, `form_name`, `form_destination`.
- **Video engagement** (`video_start`, `video_progress`, `video_complete`) for embedded YouTube players with JS API enabled.
- **File downloads** (`file_download`) for links ending in common document, archive, audio and video extensions.

These events and their parameters are reportable without creating custom dimensions, because GA4 knows them. They count toward event limits like any event.

Turn off what you do not need. Form events are the usual problem: on sites with search boxes or newsletter forms in the header, `form_start` fires constantly and clutters reports; sites with custom form frameworks may get `form_submit` without a real submission. Video events only work for YouTube iframes, not Vimeo or native `<video>`.

Enhanced measurement is a good first layer; your own custom events for sign-ups and purchases sit on top of it.
takeaways: Seven switches on the web stream give you interaction events with no code
Scroll fires only at 90%; video works only for YouTube embeds
Disable noisy switches (often form interactions) rather than filtering later
pitfalls: Expecting video events from Vimeo or a native <video> element; only YouTube embeds are supported.

quiz.q: A user scrolls to 50% of a page. Which enhanced measurement event fires?
quiz.explain: The built-in scroll event has a single 90% threshold; finer tracking needs GTM or custom code.

concepts.name: Sending custom events with gtag
concepts.summary: Use gtag('event', name, {params}) to record interactions GA4 cannot see on its own, preferring recommended names.
concepts.why: Sign-ups, leads, feature usage and anything business-specific must be sent by you.
concepts.body:
Anything that is not a page view, scroll or click needs an explicit call:

```javascript
gtag('event', 'sign_up', { method: 'email' });
```

The first argument is the event name, the second an object of parameters. Before inventing a name, check the **recommended events** list (`login`, `sign_up`, `search`, `share`, `generate_lead`, `select_content`, `tutorial_begin`, and the ecommerce set). Recommended names are not magic in themselves, but GA4 and Google Ads know their expected parameters, prebuilt reports pick them up, and predictive metrics rely on `purchase` specifically.

Rules for names and parameters:

- snake_case, letters/digits/underscores, max 40 characters, case-sensitive (`Sign_Up` and `sign_up` are two events).
- Do not prefix with `google_`, `ga_` or `firebase_`; those are reserved.
- Up to 25 custom parameters per event; values up to 100 characters; numeric values go in as numbers, not strings, if you will make a metric of them.
- Keep cardinality sane. A parameter like `search_term` is fine; a parameter holding a full URL with session tokens creates millions of distinct values and the dimension shows `(other)` in reports.

Where to fire the event: on the action that means something, usually the *success* of a form submission (after the server answers), not the button click. Attach the handler in JavaScript rather than inline `onclick`, so the tracking lives in one place.

If you use GTM, the equivalent is pushing to `dataLayer` and letting a GA4 event tag read it; the event naming rules are identical.
takeaways: gtag('event', name, params) is how you record business interactions
Prefer recommended event names; custom names are fine when nothing fits
Fire on success, keep names consistent, avoid high-cardinality parameters

quiz.q: Which event name will GA4 treat as a different event from sign_up?
quiz.explain: Event names are case-sensitive, so inconsistent casing splits your data.

quiz.q: Where should a 'form submitted' event usually fire?
quiz.explain: Firing on success avoids counting validation failures and double clicks as conversions.

concepts.name: Key events (conversions)
concepts.summary: Mark the events that represent success as key events so GA4 counts and attributes them everywhere.
concepts.why: Key events drive the key-event reports, attribution, Google Ads bidding and engaged-session logic.
concepts.body:
A **key event** is an event you have flagged as important: a purchase, a lead form, a sign-up. Until March 2024 GA4 called these *conversions*; the rename happened so that "conversion" means the same thing in Google Ads (an ad-driven key event). Older articles and the Google Ads UI still say conversions.

Marking one is a toggle, not code. In Admin > Events (or Admin > Key events) find the event name and switch **Mark as key event**. If the event has not been seen yet, create the key event by name in advance; it activates when the first one arrives. The flag is not retroactive: events before the toggle are not counted as key events.

You can have up to 30 key events per property (50 in 360). Each has a **counting method**: *once per event* (default, right for purchases) or *once per session* (right for leads, where one person submitting twice is still one lead).

Once flagged, the event appears in the *Key events* report, in acquisition reports as *Key events* and *Session key event rate*, in Explore as a metric, in the Advertising section's attribution and path reports, and, if linked, in Google Ads as an importable conversion. A session with a key event also counts as engaged.

A frequent mistake is marking `page_view` with a URL condition. GA4 cannot do that directly; instead, create a new event in Admin > Events > *Create event* that fires when `page_view` has `page_location` containing `/thank-you`, then mark that derived event as key. Better still, send an explicit `generate_lead` event from the form.
takeaways: Key event = flagged event; 'conversion' is the old name and the Google Ads name
Toggle in Admin, max 30 per property, not retroactive
Counting method: once per event (purchases) vs once per session (leads)

quiz.q: A lead form can be submitted twice in one visit. Which counting method avoids double-counting?
quiz.explain: Once per session counts the key event at most once per session regardless of repeats.

concepts.name: User properties and custom definitions
concepts.summary: Register your own parameters as custom dimensions and metrics, and describe users with user properties.
concepts.why: Without registration your parameters are collected but invisible in reports and explorations.
concepts.body:
GA4 only puts a parameter in the dimension picker once you tell it to. Admin > Custom definitions is where you do that.

A **custom dimension** maps a parameter name to a reportable dimension and has a scope:

- *Event-scoped*: the parameter is on an event (`billing_period`, `article_author`). Up to 50 per property.
- *User-scoped*: a **user property**, an attribute of the person (`plan`, `account_type`). Up to 25.
- *Item-scoped*: a custom field in an ecommerce `items` array (`item_colour`). Up to 10.

A **custom metric** maps a numeric parameter to a metric (`plan_count`, `video_seconds`) with a unit (standard, currency, distance, time). Up to 50.

User properties are sent separately from events with `gtag('set', 'user_properties', {...})` before the events they should describe; GA4 attaches the latest value to every subsequent event from that user, and reports show the value in effect at the time of each event. They are ideal for things that change rarely: subscription tier, signup cohort, language preference. Never put personal data (name, email) in them.

Registration is not retroactive. Data for a custom dimension starts from the moment you create it, even though the parameter was collected earlier; BigQuery still has the raw values for the past. Create definitions on the same day you deploy the parameter, and you cannot delete a definition for a while after use, only archive it, so name carefully.

High-cardinality dimensions (unique IDs, timestamps, long free text) blow the row limits and surface as `(other)`. Keep values categorical.
takeaways: Custom dimensions: event (50), user (25), item (10); custom metrics: 50
User properties describe the person and ride along on every later event
Registration is not retroactive; avoid high-cardinality values

quiz.q: You deployed a parameter two weeks ago and register a custom dimension today. In standard reports it shows data from...
options: Only after 48 hours, then from two weeks ago
quiz.explain: Custom definitions collect from creation time; only BigQuery has the earlier raw values.

concepts.name: Verifying with DebugView and Realtime
concepts.summary: Check that events and parameters arrive as intended before you trust a single report.
concepts.why: Reports lag by a day or more, so DebugView and Realtime are the only fast feedback loop.
concepts.body:
After any tagging change, verify it live. GA4 gives you two tools.

**Realtime** (Reports > Realtime) shows activity from the last 30 minutes: users by page, event names, key events and user source. It is enough to confirm the tag loads and the big events fire, but it shows no parameters and mixes in everyone else's traffic.

**DebugView** (Admin > DebugView) shows a single browser's event stream, second by second, with every parameter and user property, including whether an event was marked as a key event. A browser appears there only when its events carry the `debug_mode` parameter. Three ways to enable it:

- `gtag('config', 'G-...', { debug_mode: true })` on a staging build,
- the *Google Analytics Debugger* Chrome extension, which sets it for every site,
- **Tag Assistant** preview mode (tagassistant.google.com), which is the GTM debugger and also marks hits as debug.

Tag Assistant adds a second view: for each tag it shows which trigger fired, the variables resolved and the exact request sent, so it is the best tool when the question is "why did this tag not fire". Your browser's Network tab, filtered to `collect?`, shows the raw request with every parameter as query string fields and is the final word.

A verification routine: load the page (expect `page_view`, `session_start`, `first_visit` on a fresh profile); perform the action (expect your event with the right parameters and numeric types); check there are no duplicates; confirm the key event flag. Then wait 24 to 48 hours and check the Events report shows it.
takeaways: Realtime: last 30 minutes, everyone, no parameters
DebugView: one browser, every parameter, needs debug_mode
Tag Assistant / Network tab answer 'why did it not fire'

quiz.q: You see your custom event in DebugView but its parameter value is missing. Most likely cause?
options: The parameter name has a typo or the value is undefined in the gtag call
The event is not a key event
quiz.explain: DebugView shows all parameters that arrive; if one is absent, the tag did not send it.

concepts.name: UTM parameters and campaign tracking
concepts.summary: Tag your campaign URLs with utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign so GA4 attributes traffic correctly.
concepts.why: Without UTMs, email, social and paid traffic lands in Direct or Referral and your acquisition reports lie.
concepts.body:
GA4 works out where a session came from using the referrer, Google Ads auto-tagging (`gclid`), and **UTM parameters** on the landing URL. The UTM fields are query parameters you add to links you control:

- `utm_source`: the site or sender, e.g. `newsletter`, `facebook`, `partner-blog`.
- `utm_medium`: the type of channel, e.g. `email`, `cpc`, `social`, `affiliate`. This value decides the default channel group, so use the standard spellings.
- `utm_campaign`: the campaign name, e.g. `spring_sale_2026`.
- `utm_term` and `utm_content`: keyword and variant; optional.
- `utm_id`, `utm_source_platform`, `utm_creative_format`, `utm_marketing_tactic`: newer fields mainly for Google's data import features.

Values are case-sensitive, so `Email` and `email` become two rows. Agree a naming convention (lower-case, hyphens or underscores, no spaces) and keep a shared sheet of campaign names. Google's *Campaign URL Builder* page generates correctly encoded links.

In reports the values appear as *Session source*, *Session medium*, *Session campaign* (session scope) and *First user source* etc. (user scope, first ever visit). The default channel grouping maps `medium` values to channels: `email` to Email, `cpc`/`ppc`/`paidsearch` to Paid Search, `social` with a known social source to Organic Social.

Do not use UTMs on internal links; a user clicking an internal link with new UTMs is attributed to a new source mid-session. And never tag links to Google Ads with manual UTMs when auto-tagging is on; `gclid` carries far more detail.
concepts.code: Shop the sale Shop now Bad
takeaways: utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign on every link you control
utm_medium decides the channel group; use standard values like email, cpc, social
Case-sensitive; never on internal links

quiz.q: Which utm_medium value makes a session fall into the Email channel?
quiz.explain: Default channel grouping matches the medium against a fixed list; 'email' (or 'e-mail', 'e_mail', 'e mail') is required.

concepts.name: Single-page apps and cross-domain tracking
concepts.summary: Handle client-side routing and multi-domain journeys so sessions and page views stay correct.
concepts.why: These two setups are where most broken GA4 implementations live: doubled page views, self-referrals and split sessions.
concepts.body:
**Single-page applications** change the URL with the History API, so the Google tag's initial `page_view` fires once and then nothing. Two fixes:

- Enhanced measurement's *Page changes based on browser history events* fires `page_view` on `pushState`/`replaceState`/`popstate`. It is easy but naive: it fires on query-string-only changes, and `page_title` is read immediately, before your framework updates `<title>`.
- Set `send_page_view: false` in the config and send `page_view` yourself from the router's navigation hook, after the title and content are ready. Send `page_location`, `page_title` and `page_referrer` explicitly; the referrer must be the previous virtual page, not `document.referrer`, or every view appears to come from the entry page.

Never do both or every route change is counted twice.

**Cross-domain tracking** is needed when one journey spans domains (`example.com` to `checkout.example-pay.com`). Cookies are per domain, so the second domain would start a new user and a new session whose source is the first domain: a *self-referral*. Fix it in Admin > Data streams > stream > Configure tag settings > **Configure your domains**: list every domain. The tag then appends a `_gl` linker parameter to links and form posts between those domains, and the receiving page reads it to adopt the same client ID and session.

Checklist for cross-domain: all domains in the list, the same measurement ID on all of them, links are real `<a>`/`<form>` elements (JS-built navigation needs `gtag('get', ...)` to read the client ID and append `_gl` yourself), and the second domain is also in *List unwanted referrals* so it never counts as a source. Subdomains of one registered domain share cookies and need none of this.
takeaways: SPA: either the history-change switch or manual page_view with send_page_view:false, never both
Send page_referrer as the previous virtual page
Cross-domain: list all domains in tag settings; the _gl linker carries the client ID
pitfalls: Keeping the enhanced-measurement history switch on while also sending page_view manually.

quiz.q: After enabling cross-domain tracking, sessions from checkout.example-pay.com still show source example.com. What did you forget?
options: To add the second domain to the unwanted referrals list
quiz.explain: The linker joins the user; unwanted referrals stops the first domain being recorded as the session's referrer.

quiz.q: In an SPA with manual page_view events, what should page_referrer be?
quiz.explain: Using document.referrer would attribute every virtual view to the external entry referrer.

concepts.name: Reports snapshot, date ranges and comparisons
concepts.summary: Find your way around the Reports section: snapshot, Realtime, collections, dates, comparisons and filters.
concepts.why: Every report shares the same controls; learning them once makes all of GA4 readable.
concepts.body:
The **Reports** section (left nav) opens on the **Reports snapshot**, a dashboard of cards summarising users, sessions, top channels, pages, key events and automated **Insights** (anomalies and trends GA4 detected). Below it sits **Realtime**, and then **collections**: *Life cycle* (Acquisition, Engagement, Monetization, Retention), *User* (User attributes, Tech) and, for newer properties, business-objective collections such as *Generate leads* or *Drive online sales*. Each collection has *overview* reports made of cards and *detail* reports with a chart plus a table.

Controls at the top apply to every report:

- **Date range**: presets or custom; tick *Compare* to add a previous period and get % change columns. Data for today is partial, and the last 24 to 48 hours can still change.
- **Comparisons**: up to five side-by-side conditions, e.g. *Device category = mobile* vs *desktop*, or *Country = Germany*. Comparisons are applied to the whole report and survive navigation between reports, but not reload.
- **Report filter** (*Add filter* in the table toolbar): a temporary dimension filter on this report only; you cannot save it, although an editor can bake a filter into a custom report.
- **Secondary dimension** (+ next to the primary dimension in a table) adds a second breakdown column.
- The search box above tables filters rows by text.

Table rows are capped (usually 10 to 250 visible) and the table only lists the top rows; use Explore for the long tail. The *Share* button exports a report as PDF or CSV or creates a share link.

Remember that standard reports are **unsampled** and show **all time**, but can be subject to thresholding when Google signals or demographics are involved.
takeaways: Snapshot and Realtime at the top; Life cycle and User collections below
Date range with Compare, up to five comparisons, temporary report filters
Standard reports are unsampled; thresholding can still hide small rows

quiz.q: You want mobile vs desktop side by side in the Pages report. What do you use?
quiz.explain: Comparisons overlay up to five conditions on the same report; a secondary dimension would add rows, not columns.

concepts.name: Acquisition reports and channel groups
concepts.summary: User acquisition vs traffic acquisition, and how source/medium become default channel groups.
concepts.why: Acquisition is the report marketers open first; the user/session distinction trips everyone up.
concepts.body:
The **Acquisition** collection answers "where did people come from". It has two detail reports that look alike and are easy to confuse:

- **User acquisition** uses *user-scoped* dimensions: *First user source*, *First user medium*, *First user default channel group*. They describe how a user was acquired the **first time ever**, so a visitor who found you via Google a year ago and returned from an email today is still counted under Organic Search here.
- **Traffic acquisition** uses *session-scoped* dimensions: *Session source / medium*, *Session default channel group*, *Session campaign*. Each session is credited to the source that started it, so today's email visit is Email.

Use user acquisition to judge which channels bring new people, and traffic acquisition to judge which channels drive visits and key events now.

A **default channel group** is a rule-based bucket derived from source, medium and campaign: Direct, Organic Search, Paid Search, Organic Social, Paid Social, Email, Referral, Affiliates, Display, Cross-network, Organic Video, Paid Video, Organic Shopping, Paid Shopping and a few more. **Unassigned** means GA4 saw source/medium values that matched no rule, which almost always means a non-standard `utm_medium`. You can define up to two **custom channel groups** in Admin for your own buckets, without changing the default.

*Direct* means no referrer and no campaign parameters: typed URLs, bookmarks, untagged emails, many mobile apps and some privacy-stripped referrers. A large Direct share is usually a tagging gap, not loyal fans.

Typical columns: users or sessions, engaged sessions, engagement rate, average engagement time, key events and *session key event rate*.
takeaways: User acquisition = first-ever source (user scope); Traffic acquisition = this session's source
Default channel groups are rule-based buckets from source/medium/campaign
Unassigned and oversized Direct point at tagging problems

quiz.q: A user first arrived from Instagram a month ago and converts today from a newsletter link. Which report credits Email?
quiz.explain: Traffic acquisition is session-scoped; user acquisition keeps the first-ever source (Organic Social).

concepts.name: Engagement, retention and user reports
concepts.summary: Read the Events, Pages and screens, Landing page, Retention, User attributes and Tech reports.
concepts.why: These reports answer what people did once they arrived and whether they came back.
concepts.body:
The **Engagement** collection is about behaviour on the site.

- **Events**: one row per event name with event count, total users, event count per user and revenue. Click a name for its parameter breakdown cards. It is the quickest way to confirm your custom events are flowing.
- **Key events**: the same, restricted to flagged events.
- **Pages and screens**: views, users, views per user, average engagement time and key events per *Page title and screen class* (switch the primary dimension to *Page path and screen class* for URL-based rows; titles merge pages that share a title).
- **Landing page**: the first page of each session with sessions, engagement rate and key events. Rows showing `(not set)` are sessions whose first event was not a page view, often a late `session_start` from a returning tab.

The **Retention** collection shows new vs returning users over time, *user retention* curves (what share of a day's new users came back on day 1, 7, 30), *user engagement* over time and *lifetime value*. It is built from acquisition dates, so it needs a few weeks of data to be meaningful.

The **User** collection has two reports. **User attributes**: demographic details (age, gender, interests) that appear only with Google signals on and enough users to clear thresholds, plus language, country and the audiences users belong to. **Tech**: browser, OS, device category, screen resolution and app version, the place to look when one browser shows a suspicious engagement rate (usually a JS error there).

Every detail report table supports a secondary dimension and the same filters and comparisons as the rest of Reports.
takeaways: Events report: confirm custom events; Pages: titles vs paths matter
Landing page shows where sessions begin; (not set) means no page view started the session
Retention needs weeks of data; demographics need Google signals

quiz.q: Two different URLs share the title 'Product' and appear as one row. Which change separates them?
options: Switch the primary dimension to Page path and screen class
Mark page_view as a key event
quiz.explain: The default primary dimension is the page title; the path dimension distinguishes URLs.

concepts.name: Customising reports in the Library
concepts.summary: Edit report cards, dimensions and metrics, build new detail reports and organise collections in the Library.
concepts.why: The default reports rarely match your KPIs; editors can reshape them without touching Explore.
concepts.body:
Users with the *Editor* or *Administrator* role can change what the Reports section contains. Two places:

**Customise a report** (pencil icon, top right of any report). For a detail report you can change the primary and secondary dimension lists, add or remove metrics, choose chart types, add a permanent **report filter** (for example, exclude `hostname = staging.example.com`) and reorder cards. *Save* either overwrites the current report or saves a copy. For overview reports you pick which summary cards appear.

**Library** (bottom of the Reports nav) is where collections are managed. A **collection** is a group of **topics**, each a group of reports. You can:

- create a new detail report from scratch (*Create new report*): choose dimensions, metrics, charts and filters,
- create a new overview report by assembling cards from existing reports,
- create a collection, arrange topics and reports in it, and **publish** it so it appears in the left nav for everyone on the property,
- unpublish or hide the default collections if the business-objective layout fits your team better.

Some linked data only appears once you publish its collection: the *Search Console* collection stays in the Library until you add it.

Limits: a property can hold up to 150 custom detail reports and a handful of custom collections; reports are property-wide, so one person's edit changes what everyone sees. That is both the point and the risk: agree on an owner.

When a question needs more than dimensions, metrics and one filter (segments, funnels, raw rows beyond the top 250), move to Explore.
takeaways: Pencil icon customises a report; Library manages collections and new reports
Published collections appear for everyone on the property
Permanent filters live in custom reports; for segments and funnels go to Explore

quiz.q: Who sees a custom collection after you publish it?
options: Only users with the Editor role
Everyone with access to the property
quiz.explain: Reports and collections are property assets, not personal ones.

concepts.name: What explorations are
concepts.summary: Explore queries raw event data with segments, funnels and paths; it can sample and is limited to the retention window.
concepts.why: Knowing when a question belongs in Explore rather than Reports saves time and avoids misreading sampled numbers.
concepts.body:
**Explore** (left nav) is GA4's ad-hoc analysis workspace. Where standard reports read from pre-aggregated tables, explorations query the **raw event data** on the fly. That buys you things reports cannot do:

- any combination of dimensions and metrics, including nested rows and pivots,
- **segments** (subsets of users, sessions or events) and sequence conditions,
- techniques beyond tables: funnels, paths, cohorts, segment overlap, a per-user timeline, lifetime values,
- tables with up to 500 rows and export to Sheets, CSV or PDF.

The trade-offs are just as important:

- **Retention window**: explorations can only see events within your data retention setting (2 or 14 months, 50 for 360). A standard report happily shows three years; an exploration over the same range silently returns nothing older than the window.
- **Sampling**: when a query covers more than 10 million events (1 billion for 360), GA4 analyses a sample and extrapolates. An icon at the top right of each tab shows a green tick for unsampled data or a warning with the sampling percentage.
- **Thresholding** applies as in reports, and **data freshness** is the same (typically a few hours to a day).
- Explorations are personal: created by you, visible only to you unless shared, and sharing is read-only. Each user can own up to 200 explorations per property, and a property holds up to 500 shared ones.

Seven **techniques** exist: Free form, Funnel exploration, Path exploration, Segment overlap, User explorer, Cohort exploration and User lifetime. A single exploration can hold up to ten tabs mixing them, all sharing the same variables.

Rule of thumb: Reports for monitoring and known KPIs; Explore for a question you have not answered before.
takeaways: Explore queries raw events: segments, funnels, paths, cohorts, 500-row tables
Limits: retention window, sampling above 10M events, thresholding
Explorations are personal; sharing is read-only; 200 per user, 500 shared per property

quiz.q: Your retention is 2 months. An exploration with a 6-month date range shows...
options: Only the last two months of data
quiz.explain: Explorations never see events older than the retention setting; reports do.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an Explore technique?
quiz.explain: Attribution lives in the Advertising section; the seven techniques are free form, funnel, path, overlap, user explorer, cohort and lifetime.

concepts.name: The Explore workspace
concepts.summary: Variables, Tab settings and the canvas: how the three panels of an exploration fit together.
concepts.why: Every technique uses the same layout, so once you can drive one, you can drive them all.
concepts.body:
Open Explore and pick *Blank* (or a template such as *Funnel exploration* or *Free form*). The screen has three panels.

**Variables** (left) is the shopping list for the whole exploration: a name, the **date range**, and the **segments**, **dimensions** and **metrics** you have imported. Click the `+` next to each to open a picker and tick what you need; up to 20 dimensions and 20 metrics per exploration. Nothing you add here shows up yet; it just becomes available to tabs.

**Tab settings** (middle) configures the current tab: the **technique**, the visualisation, and the slots that technique offers. For a free-form table the slots are *Rows*, *Columns*, *Values* (metrics) and *Filters*; a funnel has *Steps* and *Breakdown*; a path has *Starting point* and *Node type*. You fill slots by dragging from Variables or by clicking a slot and choosing. Segments dropped here apply only to this tab, so you can compare the same table with and without a segment on two tabs.

**Canvas** (right) renders the result and updates as you change settings. Right-click a row, bar or node for actions: *Include only* / *Exclude* (creates a tab filter), *Create segment from selection*, *View users* (opens User explorer for those users).

Tabs sit across the top; duplicate a tab to branch off an analysis and keep the original. Everything auto-saves; there is no save button. Renaming the exploration and its tabs is worth the five seconds when you have twenty of them.

The sampling/thresholding indicator sits at the top right of the canvas; check it before quoting a number.

The *Share* icon makes the exploration visible read-only to others on the property; they can *Duplicate* to get an editable copy. *Export* gives Google Sheets, TSV, CSV or PDF.
takeaways: Variables = what is available; Tab settings = how this tab uses it; Canvas = result
Segments applied in Tab settings affect only that tab
Right-click the canvas to filter, segment or view users; everything auto-saves

quiz.q: You added 'Country' in Variables but the table does not change. Why?
options: Country is not available in Explore
Variables only make a dimension available; it must be placed in Rows or Columns in Tab settings
Country only works as a segment
quiz.explain: The Variables panel is a palette; Tab settings decide what the current tab shows.

concepts.name: Free-form tables
concepts.summary: Build a table with rows, columns and values, nest rows, pivot and filter: the workhorse of Explore.
concepts.why: Most analysis questions are a table; free form gives you full control over its shape.
concepts.body:
The **Free form** technique with the *Table* visualisation is where you will spend most Explore time. Tab settings slots:

- **Rows**: up to five dimensions. With more than one, they nest: *Country* then *Device category* gives a row per combination. The **Nested rows** toggle shows them as an indented tree instead of a flat list. *Start row* and *Show rows* (10 to 500) page through long lists.
- **Columns**: up to two dimensions pivoted across the top, e.g. *Month* to turn a list into a trend table or *Session default channel group* to compare channels side by side. *Show columns* limits how many values.
- **Values**: up to ten metrics. **Cell type** can be plain text, a bar chart in the cell, or a heat map, which makes outliers visible without reading numbers.
- **Filters**: up to ten conditions on dimensions or metrics (*Page path contains /blog/*, *Event count > 100*). Filters restrict the rows of this tab; they are not segments.
- **Segment comparisons**: up to four segments; the table then shows one block per segment.

A useful pattern: Rows = *Landing page + query string*, Columns = *Session default channel group*, Values = *Sessions*, *Engagement rate*, *Key events*, filter *Sessions > 50*. Sort by clicking a metric header.

Free form is also the only technique with the **Pivot** idea in a strict sense: moving a dimension from Rows to Columns is pivoting it, and the canvas updates immediately.

Remember scopes: a table with *Session source* in rows and *Users* in values asks how many users had at least one session from each source, which double-counts users across rows. That is expected, not a bug; totals in the footer are deduplicated.

Right-click any cell to drill: *Include only*, *Exclude*, *Create segment from selection*, *View users*.
takeaways: Rows (up to 5, nestable), Columns (up to 2), Values (up to 10), Filters (up to 10)
Cell type bar/heat map makes patterns visible; Show rows goes to 500
Users can be counted in several rows; the footer total is deduplicated

quiz.q: You want a row per landing page and a column per month. Where does Month go?
quiz.explain: Columns pivot a dimension across the top; Rows would instead nest months under pages.

concepts.name: Free-form charts and anomaly detection
concepts.summary: Switch a free-form tab to donut, line, scatter, bar or geo, and turn on anomaly detection on a line chart.
concepts.why: A chart answers 'is it changing?' and 'is it unusual?' faster than a table.
concepts.body:
The Free form technique has six **visualisations**; all read the same Rows/Values slots, so you can prototype in a table and flip to a chart.

- **Donut chart**: share of one metric across one dimension; the breakdown dimension is the first row dimension. Good for channel mix or device share, limited to a handful of slices with *Other*.
- **Line chart**: a metric over time. Granularity is day, week or month; the breakdown dimension (optional) draws one line per value, capped at a few top values. This is the only visualisation with **Anomaly detection**: tick it in Tab settings, set a *training period* (how many prior days to learn from, 7 to 90) and *sensitivity* (the probability threshold). Points outside the forecast band are circled, which is exactly the signal behind the Insights cards in Reports, now under your control.
- **Scatter plot**: two metrics as x and y, one point per dimension value, optionally a third metric as bubble size. Use it to find pages with high views but low engagement, or campaigns with high cost but few key events.
- **Bar chart**: horizontal bars for one metric across one dimension, with an optional breakdown.
- **Geo map**: a metric by *Country*, *Region* or *City* on a world map.

Line and bar charts honour segments as separate series, so applying two segments gives a direct visual comparison.

Two gotchas. First, charts use the same date range as the tab, and the line chart's granularity cannot exceed what the range allows. Second, `(not set)` and `(other)` rows appear in charts too; add a filter to drop them before presenting.

Export a chart as PDF, or screenshot it; charts do not export to Sheets, only tables do.
takeaways: Six visualisations share the same Rows/Values settings
Anomaly detection lives on the line chart: training period and sensitivity
Scatter plots compare two metrics per dimension value to find outliers

quiz.q: Which visualisation lets you flag unusual daily values automatically?
quiz.explain: Anomaly detection is a line-chart option that forecasts from a training period and marks outliers.

concepts.name: Funnel exploration
concepts.summary: Define ordered steps and see how many users complete each one, where they drop off, and how long it took.
concepts.why: Drop-off between steps is the most actionable number in product analytics.
concepts.body:
**Funnel exploration** answers "of the users who did A, how many went on to do B and C?". In Tab settings:

- **Steps** (up to ten): each step is a condition on an event, a dimension or a metric, e.g. *Event name = view_item*, then *add_to_cart*, then *begin_checkout*, then *purchase*. A step can have several conditions (*page_location contains /pricing* AND *device category = mobile*). Between steps you can choose *is directly followed by* (the next event the user fired) or *is indirectly followed by* (anything can happen in between, the default), and add a **within** time constraint (within 10 minutes, within 2 days).
- **Visualisation**: *Standard funnel* (bars with completion rate and abandonment per step) or **Trended funnel** (a line per step over time, so you can see whether a release moved step 3's completion).
- **Make open funnel**: see the next lesson.
- **Breakdown**: one dimension (device category, country, first user source) splitting every step into up to 15 rows.
- **Show elapsed time**: adds the average time users took between consecutive steps.
- **Next action**: shows the top five events (or page titles) users fired right after each step, which tells you where the drop-offs went instead.
- **Segments** (up to four) to compare, say, new vs returning users as separate funnels.

The canvas shows, per step, *Users* and *Completion rate*, plus *Abandonments* and *Abandonment rate* between steps. Funnels are user-based: a user who did step 2 before step 1 within the date range does not count as completing step 2.

Funnels are retroactive. Unlike Universal Analytics goal funnels, you can define a new funnel today and see last month's data, within the retention window.

Right-click a step to create a segment of users who dropped off there and send them to User explorer or build an audience from them.
takeaways: Steps are ordered event/dimension conditions; users must do them in order
Directly vs indirectly followed, time constraints, breakdown, elapsed time, next action
Retroactive within the retention window, unlike UA goal funnels

quiz.q: Step 2 is 'is directly followed by' step 3. A user fires step 2, then a scroll event, then step 3. Counted?
options: No; a different event came in between
quiz.explain: Directly followed means the very next event must match step 3; use indirectly followed to allow other events.

concepts.name: Open vs closed funnels and funnel diagnostics
concepts.summary: Choose between open and closed funnels, and use breakdown, elapsed time, next action and trends to diagnose a leak.
concepts.why: Open vs closed changes the numbers dramatically, and the diagnostic options turn a chart into a to-do list.
concepts.body:
A **closed funnel** (the default) only counts users who entered at step 1. Someone who landed directly on the checkout page is excluded, and the completion rates read as "of those who started here". It is right for designed flows such as onboarding or checkout, and for asking how good the flow is.

An **open funnel** (*Make open funnel* toggle) lets users enter at any step. A user who skipped straight to step 3 is counted at steps 3 and 4. The numbers at later steps rise, often sharply, and the funnel now answers "how many people reached this point, however they got here". Use it for loosely ordered journeys such as content paths, or when deep links and ads land people mid-flow.

When a step leaks, work through the diagnostics in order:

- **Breakdown** by *Device category* or *Browser*: a leak isolated to one platform is a bug, not a design problem.
- **Next action**: if users who abandoned checkout next fired `view_cart` or `page_view` of the shipping page, the price or a form is the issue; if they fired nothing, they left the site.
- **Elapsed time**: a step that takes users minutes instead of seconds is a confusing step.
- **Trended funnel**: did the drop appear on a specific date? Line that date up with deploys and campaign launches.
- **Segments**: compare new vs returning, or a segment of a campaign's users, as separate funnels.

Two accuracy notes. A funnel spanning sessions works because funnels are user-based, but a step condition on a session-scoped dimension (such as *Session source*) is evaluated per event's session, which can exclude users who switched sources. And funnel user counts respect the reporting identity: with User-ID, a user who added to cart on mobile and bought on desktop completes.

All funnel data is subject to the retention window and sampling like any exploration.
takeaways: Closed: must enter at step 1; open: any step; later steps grow in open funnels
Diagnose leaks with breakdown, next action, elapsed time and trended view
Funnels are user-based across sessions and devices (with User-ID)

quiz.q: Switching a checkout funnel from closed to open makes step 4 jump from 800 to 2,100 users. Why?
options: Users who entered the flow at a later step are now counted
Open funnels count sessions instead of users
quiz.explain: An open funnel admits users at any step, so people who skipped early steps add to later counts.

quiz.q: Which option tells you what abandoning users did instead?
quiz.explain: Next action lists the top events users fired right after each step, including after dropping off.

concepts.name: Segments and segment overlap
concepts.summary: Build subsets of users, sessions or events with scoped conditions, tell them apart from filters, and compare them with segment overlap.
concepts.why: Segments are how you ask 'how does this group behave?' and are the most powerful Explore feature.
concepts.body:
A **segment** is a subset of your data defined by conditions. Create one from the Variables panel (`+` next to Segments) or by right-clicking on the canvas. Besides suggested segments, custom ones come in three types:

- **User segment**: all events from users who match. *Users who purchased* includes their browsing from before the purchase.
- **Session segment**: all events from sessions that match. *Sessions from Paid Search* keeps those visits, not the same users' organic visits.
- **Event segment**: only the matching events, e.g. *purchase events with value > 100*.

Pick the scope by asking: everything about these people, everything in these visits, or only these events?

Conditions use dimensions and metrics with operators (equals, contains, regex, greater than, is one of), grouped in *Include* and *Exclude* blocks with AND/OR. Each condition group has its own **scoping**: *Across all sessions* (default for user segments), *Within the same session* or *Within the same event*. "Viewed pricing AND purchased" means something different across all sessions than within one session.

A user segment has a **Build an audience** checkbox that creates a matching audience for Google Ads; the reverse is impossible.

**Filters vs segments**: a tab filter removes rows from the output; a segment changes the population before metrics are computed, and only segments can express exclusions and sequences. A *user* segment of German users also brings their sessions from abroad; a filter *Country = DE* would not.

**Segment overlap** is the technique that draws up to three segments as a Venn diagram, with a table of every combination and the metrics you choose. Use it to check whether two groups are really the same people (mobile users vs purchasers). Right-click a region and choose **Create segment from selection** to turn an intersection into a reusable segment. Users are counted even for session and event segments, so mixing scopes is legal but easy to misread.

Segments are retroactive, which audiences are not, and up to four apply per tab.
takeaways: User, session and event segments keep different sets of events
Condition scoping (across sessions / same session / same event) changes meaning
Filters trim output rows; segments redefine the population and support exclusions
Segment overlap compares up to three segments and spawns intersection segments

quiz.q: You build a session segment 'Session medium = email'. Which events does it include?
options: Every event in sessions that started from email
All events ever from users who had an email session
Only key events in those sessions
quiz.explain: Session scope keeps whole sessions that match; user scope would keep every session of those users.

quiz.q: In a segment overlap, the 'A and B' region is blank with a warning icon. Most likely reason?
options: Data thresholding hid a small group
quiz.explain: Small user groups are withheld when thresholding applies; switch to device-based identity to check.

concepts.name: Sequence segments
concepts.summary: Define users by an ordered series of steps, with direct or indirect succession and time limits.
concepts.why: Sequences express 'did A then B' questions that neither filters nor plain conditions can.
concepts.body:
A **sequence** is a user-segment condition that requires events in a particular order. In the segment builder choose *Add sequence* (available for user segments). Each **step** is a condition group like any other; between steps you choose *is indirectly followed by* (anything may happen in between) or *is directly followed by* (the very next event must match). Up to ten steps.

Options on the sequence:

- **Sequence scoping**: *Across all sessions* (steps may span visits) or *Within the same session*.
- **Time constraint**: the whole sequence must complete within N minutes, hours or days.
- *Step 1 must be the first event*: the first step has to be the user's first event in the date range, for "first thing they did" questions.

Examples of questions only sequences answer:

- Users who viewed a product then searched (they did not find what they wanted on the page).
- Users who started checkout and, within 30 minutes, viewed the shipping-policy page before purchasing.
- Users whose first event was a `page_view` of a blog post and who later signed up.

Sequences in segments complement funnels. A funnel shows counts per step for everyone; a sequence segment captures the people who completed (or failed) a path so you can look at anything else about them: their channels, their other pages, their lifetime value, their user explorer timelines. Combine both: build the funnel, then right-click a step to spawn a sequence segment of the users who reached it.

An **Exclude** block can also hold a sequence, which is how you express "users who added to cart but never purchased" cleanly: include *add_to_cart*, exclude a sequence or condition *purchase*. Exclusion can be *temporarily* (only events after the match are excluded) or *permanently* (the whole user is excluded).

Sequences are evaluated at query time over raw events, so they obey the retention window and can trigger sampling on big properties.
takeaways: Sequences require ordered steps; direct vs indirect succession and time limits
Scope across sessions or within one session; optional 'first event' anchor
Exclude blocks express 'did A but never B'

quiz.q: Which question needs a sequence rather than a plain AND condition?
options: Users who viewed /pricing and then signed up
quiz.explain: Order matters only in the second; the others are satisfied by unordered conditions or filters.

concepts.name: Path exploration
concepts.summary: Follow what users did before or after an event or page as a tree of nodes, forwards or backwards.
concepts.why: Paths reveal journeys you did not think to put in a funnel, including dead ends and loops.
concepts.body:
**Path exploration** draws a tree: a starting node and, to its right, the most common next steps, each of which expands into its own next steps. Nodes can be one of three **node types**, chosen per column: *Event name*, *Page title and screen name* or *Page path and screen class*; you can mix them, say events for step 1 and page titles after.

Set a **starting point** (an event like `session_start` or a page) to ask "what happens next?". Or set an **ending point** instead to ask "how did people get here?"; GA4 then builds the tree backwards, which is the better question for a key event: what did purchasers do right before purchasing?

Each node shows the number of events (or users, switchable in Tab settings via *Node type* metrics) that flowed through it, with the top five branches shown and the rest in *+ more*. Click a node to expand it; the tree can grow very wide, so keep a breakdown dimension (*Device category*, *First user source*) in mind to colour nodes rather than adding columns.

Useful toggles:

- *View only unique nodes*: collapses repeated consecutive events such as `scroll, scroll, scroll`.
- Right-click a node to *Create segment from selection* or *Exclude* it; excluding noisy events like `user_engagement` and `scroll` from the node list makes paths readable. Do this early.
- A segment applied to the tab restricts whose paths are drawn.

Paths cross sessions unless you start from `session_start`. The technique is good at spotting loops (A to B back to A), unexpected exits to the help centre, and the pages that precede a conversion. It is bad at quantifying a long flow; build a funnel for that once a path has shown you which flow to measure.
takeaways: Start from an event/page to look forwards, or set an ending point to look backwards
Node types: event name, page title, page path; mixable per column
Exclude noisy events (scroll, user_engagement) first

quiz.q: You want to know which pages people viewed just before purchasing. Which setup?
options: Ending point = purchase, node type = page path
quiz.explain: An ending point builds the tree backwards from the chosen event.

concepts.name: User explorer
concepts.summary: Inspect individual users' event timelines and delete a single user's data from there.
concepts.why: Seeing one real journey end to end is the fastest way to validate a tagging plan or understand a drop-off.
concepts.body:
**User explorer** lists individual users (identified by the *App-instance ID* / client ID or your *User-ID*, shown as the *effective user ID*) with summary metrics: event count, sessions, engagement time, key events, revenue, first and last seen. Sort by any column, apply a segment to narrow the list, or arrive here by right-clicking users in another technique and choosing *View users*.

Click a row to open the **user activity** view: a vertical timeline of every event that user fired within the retention window, grouped by session, with the user's properties and acquisition details in a side card. Each event expands to show its parameters. Tick the event types you care about to declutter.

What it is good for:

- QA: find your own test user (use DebugView to learn your client ID) and check the sequence of events, parameter values and session boundaries after a release.
- Understanding a funnel drop-off: open five users who abandoned step 3 and read what they actually did.
- Support investigations when a customer reports a problem and you have their User-ID.

What it is not for: reporting. The list is capped and sampled like any exploration, and identities are pseudonymous. Do not try to build counts from it.

In the user activity view the trash icon **deletes this user's data** from the property (a per-user deletion request, processed within about 72 hours). Bulk deletion by dimension values is in Admin > Data deletion requests. There is also a per-user export in the side card, which is one way to satisfy a data-access request for a known User-ID.

User explorer honours reporting identity: under Blended, a User-ID user shows all their devices in one timeline.
takeaways: A list of pseudonymous users with a per-user event timeline
Use it for QA, drop-off forensics and support, not for counts
Trash icon deletes one user's data; bulk deletion lives in Admin

quiz.q: Which is the right tool to see every event a specific logged-in customer fired last week?
options: User explorer with a segment on their User-ID
quiz.explain: User explorer shows the per-user timeline; a segment or sort on the effective user ID finds the person.

concepts.name: Cohort and user lifetime explorations
concepts.summary: Group users by when they arrived or acted and measure their return, plus per-user lifetime value and engagement.
concepts.why: Retention and lifetime value are the metrics that separate growth from churn with a leaky bucket.
concepts.body:
**Cohort exploration** groups users by a shared starting event and shows what share of each group came back in later periods, as a triangle table.

- **Inclusion criteria**: what puts a user in a cohort. *First touch (acquisition date)* is the classic new-user cohort; *Any event*, *Any transaction*, *Any key event* or a specific event also work, so you can cohort by "first purchase".
- **Return criteria**: what counts as coming back: *Any event* (just showed up), *Any transaction*, *Any key event* or a specific event.
- **Cohort granularity**: daily, weekly or monthly; the table shows up to 60 cohorts.
- **Calculation**: *Standard* (returned in that exact period), *Rolling* (returned in that period and every period before), *Cumulative* (returned in that period or any earlier one).
- **Metric**: *Active users* by default; or a metric per cohort user such as revenue, with *Metric type* sum or per-user.

Read it row by row: week-0 cohorts are 100%, and the columns show the decay. Compare cohorts vertically: if the February cohorts retain better than January's, something changed. A **breakdown** dimension (first user channel, country) creates one triangle per value, which is where the insight usually is.

**User lifetime** is a free-form-like table restricted to users active in the date range, with lifetime metrics computed over their whole history on the property: *Lifetime value* (LTV, revenue), *Lifetime engagement duration*, *Lifetime sessions*, *Lifetime transactions*, and *First purchase date*, *Last active date*, plus the predictive metrics when available. Pair them with user-scoped dimensions such as *First user source* or *First user campaign* to see which acquisition channels produced the highest-value users, not just the most users.

Both techniques are user-based and benefit from User-ID; both respect the retention window, which caps how far back a cohort can start.
takeaways: Cohort = inclusion criteria + return criteria + granularity; read the decay
Standard vs rolling vs cumulative calculation change what 'returned' means
User lifetime: LTV and lifetime engagement by acquisition dimension

quiz.q: You want the share of each week's new users who were active in every week since. Which calculation?
quiz.explain: Rolling requires the user to have returned in each successive period, not just the one shown.

quiz.q: Which dimension answers 'which campaign brought the most valuable users'?
options: First user campaign with Lifetime value
quiz.explain: User lifetime pairs user-scoped acquisition dimensions with lifetime metrics.

concepts.name: Sampling, thresholding and precision in Explore
concepts.summary: How GA4 samples large exploration queries, how thresholding withholds rows, and what you can do about each.
concepts.why: Quoting a sampled or thresholded number as fact is the classic analyst error; know the indicators and the workarounds.
concepts.body:
Two separate mechanisms can make an exploration differ from the truth.

**Sampling** kicks in when a single query touches more than 10 million events (1 billion on 360). GA4 reads a representative subset and scales it up. The indicator at the top right of the tab shows a green tick (*This exploration is based on 100% of available data*) or a warning with the sampled percentage; hover it for the exact figure. Sampling is per query, so a narrower date range, fewer dimensions or a segment that reduces the events scanned can bring you back under the limit. Properties on 360 also get a *Data quality* toggle for *Faster results* vs *More detailed results*, trading speed for a larger sample. For the long tail (small segments, rare events), sampled results can be badly off; headline totals are usually fine.

**Thresholding** is different: rows are withheld, not estimated, to stop anyone inferring the identity or demographics of individuals. It applies when the query involves Google signals data or demographic dimensions, or when the reporting identity includes anything beyond device ID and a row would represent very few users. The indicator shows an orange icon with *Thresholding applied*. Remedies: widen the date range, remove demographic dimensions, or switch Admin > Reporting identity to Device-based (reversible, report-time only). Standard reports are also thresholded, but never sampled.

**(other)** rows are a third effect: tables with too many distinct dimension values, especially high-cardinality custom dimensions, get their tail collapsed into `(other)`. Explorations suffer less than reports but are not immune; lowering cardinality at collection time is the real fix.

And always the **retention window**: a query beyond it simply has no data, with no indicator at all.

When none of these workarounds suffice, the answer is the BigQuery export: raw, unsampled, unthresholded and kept as long as you like.
takeaways: Sampling: >10M events per query, estimated; green tick vs warning icon
Thresholding: rows withheld for privacy; fix with Device-based identity or wider range
(other) is cardinality overflow; BigQuery escapes all three

quiz.q: A row for a city with 3 users is missing from an exploration and an orange icon shows. What happened?
quiz.explain: Thresholding withholds rows that would expose a very small number of users.

quiz.q: Which change can make a sampled exploration unsampled?
quiz.explain: Sampling depends on the number of events the query scans; fewer days means fewer events.

concepts.name: A weekly analysis workflow with Explore
concepts.summary: A worked example that strings reports, free form, a funnel and a segment into a repeatable weekly review.
concepts.why: Knowing the techniques is not the same as knowing which one to reach for; a routine makes analysis habitual.
concepts.body:
Here is a weekly review for a SaaS marketing site, as a sequence of GA4 moves.

**1. Check the snapshot (5 min).** Reports snapshot with *Compare: previous period*. Note the Insights cards. Anything moved more than 20%? Write it down as a question, not an answer.

**2. Confirm the plumbing (3 min).** Events report: are `page_view`, `sign_up`, `generate_lead` counts in their normal range? A sudden zero is a broken tag, and every other number this week is suspect until it is fixed.

**3. Acquisition table (10 min).** Explore, free form. Rows: *Session default channel group*, then *Session campaign* nested. Columns: *Week*. Values: *Sessions*, *Engagement rate*, *Key events*, *Session key event rate*. Cell type: heat map. Filter *Sessions > 30*. The heat map shows which campaign's conversion rate fell.

**4. Landing pages (10 min).** Second tab, same exploration. Rows: *Landing page + query string*. Values: *Sessions*, *Engagement rate*, *Key events*. Apply a segment *Session default channel group = Paid Search* on this tab only. Sort by sessions, look for pages with engagement rate well below the tab average; those are the pages burning ad money.

**5. The funnel (10 min).** Third tab, funnel: `page_view` of `/pricing`, then `sign_up`, then `tutorial_begin`. Closed, breakdown by *Device category*, elapsed time on. Compare with last week by switching to the trended funnel. If mobile step 2 dipped, open **Next action** to see where mobile users went instead.

**6. Users (5 min).** Right-click the leaky step, *View users*, and read three timelines in User explorer.

**7. Share.** Explorations are personal, so share the exploration read-only, or export the two tables to Google Sheets. For a standing dashboard, connect **Looker Studio** to the property with its native GA4 connector; it uses the Data API, so it shares its quotas and can sample; keep dashboards to a few charts.

Save it as *Weekly review* with named tabs; next week only the date range changes.
takeaways: Snapshot and Events report first: is the data trustworthy this week?
One exploration, several tabs: acquisition heat map, landing pages with a segment, funnel with breakdown
Finish in User explorer and share or export; Looker Studio for standing dashboards

quiz.q: Why check the Events report before analysing acquisition changes?
options: A broken tag would explain every other change
quiz.explain: If a key event stopped firing, acquisition 'drops' are measurement artefacts.

quiz.q: You want a colleague to tweak your exploration. What must they do?
options: Open the shared link and edit
quiz.explain: Shared explorations are read-only; duplicating creates an editable personal copy.

concepts.name: Ecommerce events and the items array
concepts.summary: Send view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout and purchase with an items array to light up revenue reporting.
