concepts.why: Revenue, product performance and purchase funnels all depend on these exact event and parameter names.
concepts.body:
GA4 has a defined set of **ecommerce events** and only populates the Monetization reports when you use them with the right parameters. The main sequence:

- `view_item_list` and `select_item` (listing pages),
- `view_item` (product page), `add_to_cart`, `remove_from_cart`, `view_cart`,
- `begin_checkout`, `add_shipping_info`, `add_payment_info`,
- `purchase`, and `refund` for returns,
- plus `view_promotion`, `select_promotion`, `add_to_wishlist`.

Every one of them carries an **items** array: one object per product with `item_id`, `item_name` (one of the two is required), and optional `price`, `quantity`, `item_brand`, `item_category` (up to `item_category5`), `item_variant`, `item_list_name`, `coupon`, `discount`, `affiliation`, `index`, `location_id`. Up to 27 items are kept per event; you can add custom fields and register them as item-scoped custom dimensions.

Event-level parameters on `purchase`: `transaction_id` (required; GA4 deduplicates purchases with the same ID within the property), `value` (total revenue), `currency` (ISO 4217 code, required whenever `value` is sent), optional `tax`, `shipping`, `coupon`. Revenue metrics in reports come from `value`; item revenue comes from `price * quantity` per item. Keep them consistent or the two revenue figures will disagree.

Common mistakes: sending `value` without `currency` (revenue is dropped), formatting price as a string with a currency symbol, firing `purchase` on the order confirmation page without protecting against refreshes (use `transaction_id` and a server-side flag), and sending `purchase` from both the website and a server-side integration.

If you use GTM, push the same structure into `dataLayer` with an `ecommerce` object; GTM's GA4 event tag reads it. Push `{ ecommerce: null }` first so the previous event's items do not leak into the next one.
takeaways: Use the documented event names and the items array exactly
purchase needs transaction_id, value and currency
Prices are numbers; currency is an ISO code; dedupe with transaction_id

quiz.q: You send purchase with value: 59.9 but no currency. What does GA4 do with the revenue?
options: Records it as item revenue only
quiz.explain: value is only recorded when accompanied by a valid currency parameter.

quiz.q: Which parameter stops a refreshed confirmation page from counting a second purchase?
quiz.explain: GA4 deduplicates purchase events that share a transaction_id.

concepts.name: Monetization reports and item scope
concepts.summary: Read the Ecommerce purchases, Purchase journey and Checkout journey reports, and item vs event revenue.
concepts.why: Product-level questions use item-scoped data, which behaves differently from the rest of GA4.
concepts.body:
The **Monetization** collection lights up once ecommerce events arrive.

- **Overview**: total revenue, purchasers, average purchase revenue per user, items by views and purchases.
- **Ecommerce purchases**: a table keyed by *Item name* (or ID, brand, category, variant, list) with item-scoped metrics: *Items viewed*, *Items added to cart*, *Items purchased*, *Item revenue*, plus rates such as *Cart-to-view* and *Purchase-to-view*.
- **Purchase journey**: a built-in closed funnel of sessions through `view_item`, `add_to_cart`, `begin_checkout`, `purchase`, with abandonment rates and a device breakdown.
- **Checkout journey**: the same for `begin_checkout`, `add_shipping_info`, `add_payment_info`, `purchase`.
- **In-app purchases**, **Publisher ads** and **Promotions** for apps, AdSense/AdMob and `view_promotion`/`select_promotion`.

Two layers of revenue exist and must be kept straight. **Purchase revenue** (event-scoped) is the `value` of `purchase` events, and *Total revenue* adds in-app and ad revenue. **Item revenue** (item-scoped) is `price * quantity` summed over items in `purchase` events; it excludes shipping and tax, so it is normally lower. *Ecommerce revenue* equals purchase revenue.

**Item scope** means a dimension or metric describes one element of the `items` array. Item dimensions combine with item metrics and with *Event count* of ecommerce events, but putting an item dimension against sessions or users produces inflated or `(not set)` rows because one event holds many items. In Explore, item-scoped dimensions are listed under *Ecommerce* and the picker greys out incompatible metrics.

Refunds appear as *Refund amount* and reduce *Purchase revenue* in the overview when sent with the original `transaction_id`. Item-scoped custom dimensions (up to 10) extend the item table with your own attributes, such as `item_colour` or `item_supplier`.
takeaways: Ecommerce purchases is item-scoped; journeys are prebuilt funnels
Purchase revenue (event) vs item revenue (price x quantity, no shipping/tax)
Item dimensions pair with item metrics and ecommerce event counts only

quiz.q: Item revenue is 95 but purchase revenue is 100 for the same order. Why?
options: Shipping and/or tax are in value but not in items
quiz.explain: Item revenue sums price times quantity; purchase revenue is the event's value including shipping and tax.

concepts.name: Attribution models and conversion paths
concepts.summary: How GA4 credits key events to channels: data-driven and last-click models, lookback windows and the paths report.
concepts.why: Attribution decides which channels look good; the model and the dimension scope change the answer.
concepts.body:
**Attribution** is the rule for splitting credit for a key event among the touchpoints before it. GA4 offers two families (Admin > Attribution settings):

- **Data-driven** (default since 2023): a model trained on your property's paths that assigns fractional credit based on how much each touchpoint changed the probability of converting. It needs enough data; small properties fall back to last click.
- **Paid and organic last click**: 100% to the last non-direct touchpoint.
- **Google paid channels last click**: 100% to the last Google Ads click if there is one, else last non-direct click. Mainly for comparing with Google Ads' own reporting.

First-click, linear, time-decay and position-based were removed in 2023.

**Lookback window** controls how far back touchpoints count: *acquisition key events* (`first_open`, `first_visit`) 7 or 30 days; all other key events 30, 60 or 90 days. Changing the model or window re-attributes historical data in reports, but not in already-exported BigQuery tables.

The choice of **dimension scope** matters as much as the model. *Session source / medium* credits the session in which the key event happened, regardless of model. *First user source* credits the first ever visit. The attribution model only applies to **attribution-scoped dimensions**, which are the plain *Source*, *Medium*, *Campaign* and *Default channel group* you find in the Advertising section and in Explore under *Attribution*; use those with *Key events* or *Total revenue* to see model-based credit.

The **Advertising** section (left nav) holds the attribution reports: *Model comparison* (same key event under two models side by side, with % change per channel), *Key event paths* (sequences of touchpoints, their count, days and touchpoints to key event, split into early/mid/late), and *Attribution* overview. Set the key event filter at the top of each report; the default is all key events combined.

A channel that gains credit under data-driven but loses under last click is an assisting channel: it introduces people who convert later via something else.
takeaways: Data-driven is the default; last-click variants are the alternatives
Lookback 30/60/90 days; model changes re-attribute reports, not exports
Models only affect attribution-scoped dimensions; session and first-user dimensions are fixed rules

quiz.q: Which dimension's values change when you switch the attribution model?
quiz.explain: Only attribution-scoped dimensions are computed by the model; session and user ones are rule-based.

quiz.q: Under data-driven, Organic Social gets 20% more credit than under last click. What does that suggest?
options: It is the final touch for most buyers
It assists conversions that close elsewhere
quiz.explain: Data-driven rewards touchpoints that raise the chance of a later conversion even when they are not last.

concepts.name: Linking Google Ads and Search Console
concepts.summary: Connect Google Ads for cost and conversion sharing, and Search Console for queries and organic landing pages.
concepts.why: The links turn GA4 into the place where ad spend, organic queries and on-site behaviour meet.
concepts.body:
Both links live in Admin > **Product links** and need you to be an Editor in GA4 and an administrator of the other product.

**Google Ads link**. Choose the Ads account (or manager account), keep *Enable personalised advertising* on if you want GA4 audiences available for remarketing, and *Enable auto-tagging* so clicks carry a `gclid`. The link does three things: GA4 reports gain a *Google Ads* set of dimensions (campaign, ad group, keyword, cost, clicks, CPC) in Acquisition and Advertising; Google Ads can **import key events** from GA4 as conversions for bidding (Tools > Conversions > Import in Ads); and GA4 audiences appear in the Ads audience manager. Data flows from the moment of linking, not retroactively, except that `gclid` sessions already collected get Ads dimensions once linked.

**Search Console link**. One Search Console property can link to one GA4 web stream. It adds two reports under a *Search Console* collection that you must **publish from the Library**: *Queries* (search query, clicks, impressions, CTR, average position; no GA4 behaviour metrics) and *Google organic search traffic* (landing page with Search Console metrics joined to GA4 engagement and key events). Search Console data lags two to three days and is limited to the last 16 months.

The Ads link has a quota: 400 Ads accounts per property. Other product links available are BigQuery, Display & Video 360, Search Ads 360, Merchant Center, Google Play, Ad Manager and Floodlight.

After linking Ads, check the *Google Ads* channel appears correctly as *Paid Search* / *Paid Social* / *Cross-network* in Traffic acquisition (Performance Max lands in Cross-network) and that cost data appears in the *Advertising* section.
takeaways: Ads link: cost and campaign dimensions in GA4, key events importable into Ads, audiences shared
Search Console link: queries and organic landing page reports, publish from the Library
Links are not retroactive and Search Console covers 16 months with a short lag

quiz.q: After linking Search Console you cannot find its reports. What is missing?
options: Publishing the Search Console collection in the Library
quiz.explain: The Search Console collection is created unpublished; an editor must add it to the nav.

concepts.name: Building audiences
concepts.summary: Define groups of users in Admin for reporting, triggers and remarketing, and understand how they differ from segments.
concepts.why: Audiences are what you export to Google Ads and what audience triggers and comparisons are built on.
concepts.body:
An **audience** (Admin > Audiences) is a saved user-group definition that GA4 evaluates continuously: as users meet the conditions they join, and after the **membership duration** (default 30 days, max 540, or *no limit*) without re-qualifying they drop out. Unlike a segment, an audience is **not retroactive**: it fills from creation onward, and the initial population only includes users who match in the next 30 days of activity. Create audiences early.

The builder is the same as the segment builder: include and exclude condition groups, scoping (across all sessions / within the same session / within the same event), and **sequences**. You can start from suggested audiences (purchasers, recently active, by template) or from a user segment in Explore with *Build an audience* ticked. Up to 100 audiences per property (400 for 360); archived ones do not count.

Where audiences show up:

- as a dimension *Audience name* in reports and Explore, and as a comparison condition,
- in the *Audiences* report under User attributes with users, sessions and revenue per audience,
- in **Google Ads** (if linked with personalised advertising on) for remarketing, observation and exclusion lists; in Display & Video 360 and Search Ads 360 via their links,
- in **Firebase** for app messaging and remote config.

**Audience triggers**: in the audience editor, *Create new* under *Audience trigger* names an event that GA4 fires when a user joins (optionally every time they re-qualify). Mark that event as a key event and you have turned a behavioural pattern, like "viewed three product pages and spent five minutes", into a conversion that Google Ads can bid on. Triggered events cost nothing and do not need code.

Audiences built on Google signals (demographics, interests) are usable for remarketing only when signals is on; such audiences also make thresholding more likely.
takeaways: Audiences are evaluated continuously, not retroactive; set membership duration
Same builder as segments, including sequences; 100 per property
Audience triggers fire an event on join, which can be a key event

quiz.q: You create an audience 'purchased in the last 30 days' today. Who is in it tomorrow?
options: Everyone who purchased in the last 30 days
Only users who purchased since creation, plus those who show up and match
quiz.explain: Audiences are not retroactive; they populate from new activity after creation.

quiz.q: What does an audience trigger do?
options: Fires a GA4 event when a user joins the audience
quiz.explain: The trigger emits an event you name, which can then be a key event for Ads bidding.

concepts.name: Predictive metrics and audiences
concepts.summary: Purchase probability, churn probability and predicted revenue, and the ready-made predictive audiences.
concepts.why: Targeting likely buyers and likely churners before they act is the most direct business use of GA4's modelling.
concepts.body:
GA4 trains models on your own property's data to compute three **predictive metrics** per user:

- **Purchase probability**: chance of a `purchase` (or `in_app_purchase`) event in the next 7 days, for users active in the last 28 days.
- **Churn probability**: chance an active user will *not* be active in the next 7 days.
- **Predicted revenue**: expected revenue from purchases in the next 28 days from users active in the last 28 days.

Eligibility is strict. The property needs the purchase (or `in_app_purchase`) event, at least 1,000 returning users who triggered it and 1,000 who did not over a 7-day window in the last 28 days, and the model must keep passing quality checks; otherwise the metrics are unavailable and Admin > Audiences shows the predictive templates as ineligible. Churn probability needs only the activity data, so it is often available before purchase probability.

You use them in two places:

- **Predictive audiences** (Admin > Audiences > *Suggested* > *Predictive*): *Likely 7-day purchasers*, *Likely 7-day churning users*, *Predicted 28-day top spenders*, *Likely first-time 7-day purchasers*, *Likely 7-day churning purchasers*. Each is a prebuilt condition on a percentile of the metric (top 10% by default) that you can edit before saving.
- As conditions in your own audiences and in **Explore** user segments: *Purchase probability > 80th percentile*; and as metrics in User lifetime (*Purchase probability*, *Churn probability*, *Predicted revenue*).

Typical activation: export *Likely 7-day purchasers* to Google Ads with higher bids, show a retention offer to *Likely churning purchasers*, or exclude *Predicted top spenders* from discount campaigns.

The metrics refresh daily and are modelled, so treat them as rankings rather than precise probabilities, and expect them to disappear if traffic drops below the thresholds.
takeaways: Purchase probability, churn probability, predicted revenue, per user, 7/28-day horizons
Needs 1,000 converting and 1,000 non-converting returning users in 7 days
Use via predictive audiences, custom audience conditions and User lifetime

quiz.q: Churn probability is available but purchase probability is not. Most likely reason?
options: The property lacks enough purchase events to train the model
quiz.explain: Purchase probability needs 1,000 purchasers and 1,000 non-purchasers; churn only needs activity data.

concepts.name: BigQuery export
concepts.summary: Export raw events to BigQuery daily or streaming, understand the nested schema and why it escapes sampling and retention.
concepts.why: BigQuery is the escape hatch from every GA4 limit and the way to join analytics with your own data.
concepts.body:
Admin > Product links > **BigQuery links** connects the property to a Google Cloud project. Pick a dataset location, the data streams to include, and the export types:

- **Daily**: a table `events_YYYYMMDD` per day, finalised a few hours after midnight in the property's time zone (and occasionally rewritten within 72 hours). Free properties get up to 1 million events per day.
- **Streaming**: `events_intraday_YYYYMMDD`, updated within minutes, deleted once the daily table lands. No event cap, but Cloud charges apply.
- **User data** export: `pseudonymous_users_` and `users_` tables with per-user attributes, audiences and lifetime metrics.

The export starts from link creation; nothing earlier is backfilled. BigQuery's own costs are modest for most sites: storage is cheap and queries are billed per byte scanned, so always filter on the table suffix (`_TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20260901' AND '20260930'`).

The **schema** is one row per event with nested, repeated fields: `event_date`, `event_timestamp` (microseconds), `event_name`, `event_params` (an array of `{key, value: {string_value, int_value, float_value, double_value}}`), `user_pseudo_id`, `user_id`, `user_properties` (same shape), `device`, `geo`, `traffic_source` (first-touch), `session_traffic_source_last_click`, `ecommerce` and `items` (array). You read a parameter with `UNNEST` and a subquery, as in the example.

Why it matters: BigQuery data is **unsampled**, **unthresholded**, **unaffected by retention** (you keep it as long as you pay for storage), carries every parameter whether or not a custom dimension exists, and can be joined to CRM, cost or product tables. Sessions, engagement rate and attribution are *not* precomputed; you rebuild them from `ga_session_id` and `engagement_time_msec`, and numbers will differ slightly from the UI, which applies identity stitching and modelling you do not get here.

Connect Looker Studio or any BI tool to the resulting tables for dashboards that never sample.
concepts.code:
-- Sessions and page views per landing page, September 2026
SELECT
  (SELECT value.string_value FROM UNNEST(event_params) WHERE key = 'page_location') AS page_location,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CONCAT(user_pseudo_id, '-',
        (SELECT value.int_value FROM UNNEST(event_params) WHERE key = 'ga_session_id'))) AS sessions,
  COUNTIF(event_name = 'page_view') AS page_views,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id) AS users
FROM `my-project.analytics_123456789.events_*`
WHERE _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20260901' AND '20260930'
  AND event_name IN ('page_view', 'session_start')
GROUP BY page_location
ORDER BY sessions DESC
LIMIT 20;
takeaways: Daily and streaming event tables, plus user tables; starts at link time
Nested schema: UNNEST event_params to read a parameter
Unsampled, unthresholded, unlimited retention; sessions must be rebuilt by hand

quiz.q: How do you read the page_location parameter of an event row in BigQuery?
options: It is a top-level column named params.page_location
A subquery over UNNEST(event_params) filtering key = 'page_location'
quiz.explain: Parameters are an array of key/value structs that you unnest and filter.

quiz.q: Which GA4 limitation does the BigQuery export NOT remove?
quiz.explain: BigQuery rows carry raw IDs; the UI's blended identity and modelling are not reproduced.

concepts.name: The Measurement Protocol
concepts.summary: Send events to GA4 from a server with an HTTP POST, to augment (not replace) browser data.
concepts.why: Offline conversions, refunds and server-side events need it, and its limitations surprise people.
concepts.body:
The **Measurement Protocol** (MP) is an HTTP endpoint that accepts GA4 events from anywhere: your backend, a payment webhook, a CRM, a kiosk. You POST JSON to `https://www.google-analytics.com/mp/collect` with two query parameters: the stream's `measurement_id` and an `api_secret` created under Admin > Data streams > stream > *Measurement Protocol API secrets*.

The body contains a `client_id` (the `_ga` cookie value, obtainable in the browser with `gtag('get', 'G-...', 'client_id', cb)`) or a `user_id`, optional `user_properties`, `consent`, a `timestamp_micros` (up to 72 hours in the past), and an `events` array of up to 25 events, each with `name` and `params`. For the events to attach to the user's live session include `session_id` and `engagement_time_msec` in `params`; otherwise they count toward the user but not toward sessions or engagement.

What MP is for: completing a journey the browser cannot see, such as a `purchase` confirmed by a payment provider, a `refund`, a lead marked *qualified* in the CRM, or an app event from a server. Google's intended use is **augmentation**; it is not designed as a full server-side replacement for the tag.

What it cannot do: MP events carry no automatic parameters, so `page_location`, `device`, `geo` (derived from the request IP, which will be your server's), referrer and campaign are absent unless you set what you can. They are not shown in Realtime's user-source cards, do not create `first_visit`, and are ignored if the event name or parameters break the rules. Attribution of an MP purchase works only if the `client_id` matches a browser that already had sessions.

Validate with the debug endpoint `/debug/mp/collect`, which returns validation messages instead of silently accepting the payload like the real endpoint does. Keep the api_secret on the server; anyone holding it can inject events into your property.
takeaways: POST JSON to /mp/collect with measurement_id and api_secret; up to 25 events per request
Use the browser's client_id plus session_id to attach to the live session
Augmentation only: no automatic parameters, geo or referrer; validate on /debug/mp/collect

quiz.q: An MP purchase shows up in Events but not in Traffic acquisition. Why?
options: It was sent without the matching session_id, so it is not tied to a session
Purchases cannot be sent via MP
quiz.explain: Without session_id (and engagement_time_msec) an MP event is user-level only and gets no session source.

quiz.q: Why use /debug/mp/collect?
options: It returns validation errors; the real endpoint accepts anything silently
quiz.explain: The production endpoint always returns 2xx; the debug endpoint tells you what is wrong.

concepts.name: Data filters: internal and developer traffic
concepts.summary: Exclude your own team's and developers' hits with traffic_type rules and data filters, carefully, because filtering is permanent.
concepts.why: Office traffic can be a large share of sessions on a small site and silently distorts every metric.
concepts.body:
GA4 has exactly two kinds of **data filter** (Admin > Data filters), up to ten per property:

- **Internal traffic**: excludes events whose `traffic_type` parameter has a value you choose (default `internal`).
- **Developer traffic**: excludes events that carry `debug_mode` (that is, anything DebugView would show).

The `traffic_type` value is set by a rule, not by you in code: Admin > Data streams > stream > Configure tag settings > **Define internal traffic**. A rule matches IP addresses (single, ranges, CIDR) and sets `traffic_type = internal`. Because the match happens in the tag server-side, it works for GTM and gtag alike. You can create several rules with different values (`internal`, `agency`) and a filter per value.

Every filter has a **state**:

- *Testing*: nothing is excluded, but matching events get the dimension *Test data filter name* so you can see in a report what *would* be removed. Start here.
- *Active*: matching events are dropped before processing. **Permanently.** There is no way to recover filtered data later, not even in BigQuery (the export happens after filtering).
- *Inactive*: switched off.

A filter applies only from the moment it is active; it never removes historical data. Check the test dimension for a week, confirm the counts look like your team and not your customers, then activate.

What data filters cannot do: filter by hostname, country, bot signature or URL. For those, use report filters, custom reports with a baked-in filter, or segments in Explore. Known bots and spiders are excluded automatically and cannot be turned off.

Remote workers' home IPs change; for them, a GTM-set `traffic_type` based on a cookie, or simply the developer filter during QA, is more reliable than IP rules.
takeaways: Two filter types: internal (traffic_type) and developer (debug_mode)
IP rules in tag settings set traffic_type; filters exclude it
Test first; Active is permanent and never retroactive

quiz.q: You activate an internal traffic filter today. What happens to last month's office sessions?
options: They move to a Test dimension
Nothing; filters only affect new events
quiz.explain: Data filters act on incoming events only; historical data is unchanged.

concepts.name: Data retention and deletion requests
concepts.summary: Choose 2 or 14 months of event retention, understand what it does and does not affect, and delete data on request.
concepts.why: The default 2-month setting quietly caps every exploration; the deletion tools are how you meet privacy obligations.
concepts.body:
Admin > Data collection and modification > **Data retention** controls how long GA4 keeps **user-level and event-level** data: **2 months** (the default) or **14 months**; 360 properties can choose 26, 38 or 50. There is also a *Reset user data on new activity* toggle that restarts the clock for a user each time they return.

What it affects: explorations, audiences built on past behaviour, and anything else that reads raw events, such as User explorer and cohort tables. An exploration whose date range reaches further back than the window simply has no data there.

What it does not affect: standard reports. They are built from aggregated tables that are kept regardless, so your Acquisition report for two years ago still works. Age, gender, and interest data is always deleted after two months no matter what you pick, and the BigQuery export is unaffected because the data already left.

Set 14 months on day one. There is no cost, and the change is not retroactive: raising it later does not bring back the months already expired.

**Deleting data** has three routes:

- **Data deletion requests** (Admin): remove all parameters, selected parameters, selected user properties or all events of a certain name in a date range, for the whole property. There is a 7-day grace period in which you can cancel; after it the deletion runs and is permanent, and it also affects standard reports.
- **Per-user deletion**: the trash icon in User explorer, or the User Deletion API for automation, for "delete my data" requests when you know the client ID or User-ID.
- **Deleting the property** moves it to a 35-day trash before permanent removal.

All deletion requests are logged in the property's change history, which auditors like.
takeaways: 2 or 14 months; affects explorations and user-level data, not standard reports
Set 14 months immediately; the change is not retroactive
Data deletion requests (property-wide, 7-day grace) vs per-user deletion

quiz.q: A standard report for 18 months ago still shows data although retention is 2 months. Is that a bug?
options: Only if Google signals is on
No; standard reports use aggregated tables unaffected by retention
quiz.explain: Retention governs raw event/user data used by explorations, not the aggregates behind reports.

concepts.name: Consent mode v2 and privacy settings
concepts.summary: Set consent defaults before the tag loads, update them from your banner, and know GA4's privacy controls.
concepts.why: Consent handling is legally required in many regions and decides whether GA4 can model the users who say no.
concepts.body:
**Consent mode** is the mechanism by which the Google tag adapts to a user's consent choices. Four consent types matter for GA4 and Ads: `analytics_storage` (GA cookies), `ad_storage` (ads cookies), and the two added in **v2** (late 2023, required for EEA audiences from March 2024): `ad_user_data` (send user data to Google for advertising) and `ad_personalization` (remarketing).

The protocol has two calls. `gtag('consent', 'default', {...})` must run **before** the Google tag loads, setting each type to `denied` or `granted`, optionally per `region` and with `wait_for_update` (milliseconds to wait for the banner's answer before sending anything). When the user chooses, your banner calls `gtag('consent', 'update', {...})`. Consent management platforms (Cookiebot, OneTrust, Usercentrics, Google's own template in GTM) issue these calls for you; your job is to make sure the default runs first and the update runs on every page load with the stored choice.

Two implementation levels:

- **Basic**: tags do not load at all until consent; no data from decliners.
- **Advanced**: tags load with denied defaults and send **cookieless pings** (no identifiers stored). GA4 uses those pings to run **behavioural modelling**, filling in estimated sessions and key events for the consented-but-missing population in reports (Blended identity). Modelling needs enough volume: roughly 1,000 denied-consent events per day for 7 of the last 28 days.

Other privacy controls in GA4: IP addresses are **never logged or stored** in GA4 (anonymisation is not a setting; it is the design), with EU traffic processed on EU servers; **Google signals** and **Granular location and device data collection** can be turned off per region under Admin > Data collection; *Ads personalisation* can be disabled per region; data-sharing settings on the account; data retention and deletion from the previous lesson; and the ability to disable collection entirely with `window['ga-disable-G-XXXX'] = true`.

Verify in DebugView: each event shows its consent state, and Tag Assistant's consent tab shows the default and update sequence.
concepts.code:
<script>
  window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || [];
  function gtag(){ dataLayer.push(arguments); }

  // 1. Defaults BEFORE the Google tag loads: deny everything in the EEA/UK, wait 500 ms for the banner
  gtag('consent', 'default', {
    ad_storage: 'denied', ad_user_data: 'denied', ad_personalization: 'denied',
    analytics_storage: 'denied',
    region: ['AT', 'BE', 'DE', 'FR', 'IT', 'ES', 'NL', 'GB', 'CH' /* ...rest of EEA */],
    wait_for_update: 500
  });
  gtag('consent', 'default', { ad_storage: 'granted', ad_user_data: 'granted',
                               ad_personalization: 'granted', analytics_storage: 'granted' });
</script>
<script async src="https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js?id=G-ABC123XYZ"></script>
<script>
  gtag('js', new Date());
  gtag('config', 'G-ABC123XYZ');

  // 2. Called by your cookie banner, and again on every page load with the stored choice
  function onConsent(choice) {
    gtag('consent', 'update', {
      analytics_storage: choice.analytics ? 'granted' : 'denied',
      ad_storage: choice.ads ? 'granted' : 'denied',
      ad_user_data: choice.ads ? 'granted' : 'denied',
      ad_personalization: choice.ads ? 'granted' : 'denied'
    });
  }
</script>
takeaways: Four consent types; v2 added ad_user_data and ad_personalization
'default' before the tag loads, 'update' from the banner, on every page
Advanced mode sends cookieless pings that power behavioural modelling

quiz.q: Where must gtag('consent', 'default', ...) be called?
options: Before the Google tag script loads
quiz.explain: Defaults must exist before any tag fires so nothing is stored or sent without permission.

quiz.q: Which consent type did consent mode v2 add?
quiz.explain: v2 added ad_user_data and ad_personalization; the storage types predate it.

concepts.name: Data-quality forensics
concepts.summary: Diagnose duplicate tags, self-referrals, unwanted referrals, missing campaigns, (not set) and bot traffic from their fingerprints.
concepts.why: Every GA4 property eventually has one of these problems; recognising the symptom saves days of guessing.
concepts.body:
Here are the recurring faults and how each one looks.

**Duplicate tagging.** Symptoms: *Views per session* near an even number, engagement rate near 100%, `page_view` count roughly double `session_start`. Confirm in the Network tab: two `collect?` requests with `en=page_view` per load. Causes: theme plus plugin, GTM plus hard-coded snippet, the SPA history switch plus manual `page_view`.

**Self-referrals.** Your own domain in *Session source*. Causes: cross-domain not configured, a payment or SSO hop, a subdomain on a different measurement ID, or redirects stripping the `_gl` parameter. Fix the domain list and add the hop to *List unwanted referrals*.

**Unwanted referrals.** `paypal.com`, `stripe.com`, `accounts.google.com` as top sources, stealing credit from the real channel and splitting sessions. Add them to the unwanted referrals list in tag settings; GA4 then ignores them as referrers.

**Unassigned channel.** Non-standard `utm_medium`, or source set but medium missing. Pull *Session source / medium* for Unassigned rows and fix the links; optionally map them in a custom channel group.

**(not set)** in landing page: sessions that began without a `page_view` (late `session_start`, an MP event). In custom dimensions: the parameter is missing on some events.

**Bot and spam traffic.** Known bots are filtered automatically, but spikes of 1-second sessions from a single city, one browser version and 100% new users are typical of scrapers; segment them out with a hostname/country/browser condition and consider server-side blocking. GA4 has no custom bot filter and no hostname filter, so a data filter cannot help.

**Hostname leaks.** Staging, localhost or a scraper copying your HTML sends data to your property. Pull *Hostname* in Explore and exclude it in custom reports or with a GTM trigger condition.

**Numbers differ from the backend.** Expect 5-15% fewer purchases in GA4 than in your order system (ad blockers, consent, tag timing); investigate beyond that by comparing `transaction_id` lists in BigQuery.

Order of investigation: Network tab, then DebugView, then Explore with *Hostname*, *Page referrer* and *Session source / medium*.
takeaways: Doubled page views: look for two collect requests per load
Self-referrals and payment-gateway referrals: domain list and unwanted referrals
No hostname/bot data filters exist; use segments, custom reports and GTM conditions

quiz.q: Engagement rate is 98% and views per session is 2.0 on a brochure site. First suspicion?
quiz.explain: Two page views per session on every visit makes every session engaged and is the classic double-tag fingerprint.

quiz.q: stripe.com is your third-largest traffic source. What fixes it?
options: Adding stripe.com to List unwanted referrals
quiz.explain: Unwanted referrals tells the tag to ignore that domain as a referrer so the original session continues.

concepts.name: Launch checklist and access roles
concepts.summary: A pre-launch checklist for a new GA4 property, including who gets which role.
concepts.why: Most GA4 regrets come from settings that are not retroactive; this list front-loads them.
concepts.body:
Settings that cannot be fixed retroactively go first.

**Property**

- Time zone and currency set before data arrives (changing them later skews daily totals).
- **Data retention: 14 months.**
- Google signals: decide per legal advice; if on, expect thresholding.
- Reporting identity: Blended, or Observed if you want no modelling.
- Enhanced measurement: switch off noisy items (often form interactions).
- Unwanted referrals: payment, SSO and login providers.
- Cross-domain list if the journey spans domains.
- Internal traffic rule for office IPs; filter in *Testing* for a week, then *Active*.
- Session timeout and engaged-session threshold if the defaults do not fit.

**Measurement plan**

- A written list of events, parameters and the business question each answers, using recommended names where they exist.
- Custom dimensions and metrics created the same day the parameters ship.
- Key events marked, with the right counting method; at most 30.
- Consent mode defaults and banner wired before any tag loads.
- Verified in DebugView on desktop and mobile; no duplicates; purchases match a test order.

**Integrations**

- Google Ads link with auto-tagging; import key events into Ads.
- Search Console link and its collection published.
- BigQuery link on day one: export is never backfilled.

**Access** (Admin > Account or Property access management). Roles are cumulative and can be granted at account or property level:

- **Viewer**: reports and explorations, no changes to settings.
- **Analyst**: Viewer plus creating and sharing explorations and other shared assets.
- **Marketer**: Analyst plus audiences, key events, custom definitions and attribution settings.
- **Editor**: everything on the property except managing users.
- **Administrator**: everything including users.

Two data restrictions stack on any role: *No cost metrics* and *No revenue metrics*. Give agencies Marketer, developers Editor during setup, and keep two Administrators.

Finally, write down the measurement ID, property ID and account owner.
takeaways: Fix non-retroactive settings first: time zone, currency, retention, BigQuery link
Measurement plan, custom definitions and key events before launch; verify in DebugView
Roles: Viewer, Analyst, Marketer, Editor, Administrator, plus cost/revenue restrictions

quiz.q: Which setting will you regret most if left at the default for six months?
quiz.explain: Retention is not retroactive, so six months of exploration-level data will be gone for good.

quiz.q: An agency needs to build audiences and mark key events but must not add users. Which role?
quiz.explain: Marketer covers audiences, key events, custom definitions and attribution without user management.
